title: Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology
answer: Detection and triage, synthetic imaging, 3D anatomical models, ultrasound enhancement and radiomics.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
children.blurb: Pathology detection and scan triage covers AI systems that examine radiology images such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs and ultrasound studies to identify suspicious findings, and that reorder radiologist worklists so urgent cases are read first.

children.name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
children.blurb: Synthetic imaging from existing scans is the practice of generating new medical images, or new contrast or modality views, from one or more already acquired scans.

children.name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
children.blurb: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology turn CT and MRI scans into physical, patient-specific replicas of organs, bones, and vascular structures.

children.name: Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement
children.blurb: Point of care ultrasound enhancement covers AI software that helps a clinician acquire, interpret, and act on ultrasound images at the bedside.

children.name: Radiomics
children.blurb: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images such as CT, MRI, and PET scans.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in diagnostic imaging now performs a set of concrete tasks rather than reading whole scans on its own. Software flags suspected lung nodules, intracranial hemorrhages, fractures and breast lesions on CT, MRI and X-ray images, and it reorders worklists so urgent cases are seen first. Some systems create synthetic CT images from MRI scans to help with radiation planning or attenuation correction. Others turn scan data into segmented 3D models for surgical planning or 3D printing, sharpen portable ultrasound images in real time, and extract radiomic features such as texture and shape for research. These tools run inside or alongside existing radiology software, and a radiologist still signs the report.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most mature work is in narrow detection and triage tasks where large, well labeled datasets exist, such as lung nodule detection on chest CT and stroke triage on head CT. What is not solved is general image interpretation, rare or subtle findings, and consistent performance across different scanners, hospitals and patient populations. Radiomics remains largely a research method because feature values change with scan settings and reconstruction, which limits reproducibility. Synthetic imaging can introduce artifacts or hallucinate structures that were not in the original scan, so it is used carefully. Across the 1000 medical AI models this site tracks, only a subset have regulatory clearance for diagnostic use, and six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies show that missed findings remain a real risk.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage is the page to start with for current clinical use, since it covers the tools that flag findings and prioritize cases. Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans and Anatomical Models and 3D Printing sit next to each other because both create something new from an existing scan, one a derived image and the other a physical or digital model. Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement covers a different workflow, where AI cleans up lower quality portable ultrasound in emergency or bedside settings. Radiomics is the most research oriented page, explaining how quantitative features are extracted and used to build predictive models, and it connects back to detection because those features often feed the same algorithms. A reader looking for what is deployed today would start with the first page, while someone interested in research pipelines would end with Radiomics.
